Voting can imply concent, but it doesn't necessarily. If you were to always vote for the candidates that are most likely to win, then that would imply consent and that you're satisfied with the establishment.

The civil way to opose the whole establishment is to always vote for the most viable non-incumbent, or in the case of no incumbent or an extremely disfavored incumbent, voting for the most viable non-incumbent candidate that is unlikely to win. If any likeminded candidates exist, I'd think you should probably support and vote for them, but I'm not entirely sure.

Voting out a large number of incumbents is interpreted as a vote of no confidence. The more times in a row that it happens, the stronger the message. Continuously voting out all the incumbents will eventually result in the establishment being changed, but pulling it off would be roughly as difficult as establishing a new viable political party.

Conventional wisdom would suggest that you need to have a more specific solution, but focusing only on dissatisfaction without a specified solution, should in theory allow you to form a coalition of dissatisfied citizens across the whole political spectrum. Unfortunately, although plenty of people are dissatisfied with both of the major parties, many of those people are sufficiently more dissatisfied with one party that they are not willing to replace an incumbent with a candidate from the more dissatisfactory party. But I don't know the numbers, so who knows, maybe it could be done.

I'd think that the core of your constituency would consist of self identified independents, but I imagine dissatisfied centrists and extreme leaning individuals from both parties may also be willing to join your coalition party.

Oh, oh! Let's call it the Anti Incumbency Coalition! That way we can market it towards people who are dissatisfied with everything and also people who are more dissatisfied with one party than another. If it caught on, we'd only ever have never before elected candidates run for election and incumbents wouldn't even try. It wouldn't necessarily destroy the established parties although it could, but it would make it harder the establishment to entrench politicians who have been bought. They'd have to try to buy off all the candidates every election cycle and reliably promise to keep paying them off after they leave office. It would be so expensive that it might just run them dry!

Edit: My initial idea was the Lame Duck Coalition and I also considered Non-Incumbent and Anti Incumbant, but I think Anti Incumbency is best. You could also call it the Anti Establishment Coalition, which sounds a bit catchier, but doesn't instantly communicate the purpose like Anti Incumbent. Although Anti Establishment does communicate the goal instantly, so it could perhaps be just as good or better. What do you think?

Edit: Although Anti Establishment probably sounds much better to some people, I think it could alienate people who only oppose the effects of incumbency without any desire to uproot the whole establishment. So I think Anti Incumbency would be more effective.
